figures.caption: Fig.1.1   Disciplines related to IA and UX design
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and UX Design: Definitions and Scope
figures.title: Disciplines supporting IA and UX
bullets: IA and UX draw on usability, information science, human factors, interaction, and visual design.
Information structure and interface behavior jointly shape the experience.
Coordinate these disciplines so people can find information and complete tasks.

figures.caption: Fig.2.1   A photo of the author’s desk in the Web1.0 era
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and Evolving Information Spaces
figures.title: The Web1.0 desktop
bullets: The desktop, wired peripherals, and desk phone show a place-bound computing experience.
Early web access was intermittent; people were often disconnected away from the desk.
This historical baseline helps explain the shift toward continuous, cross-device access.

figures.caption: Fig.2.2   Diagram   for   a   mashup   of   the   US   Government’s   publicly   accessible   MedlinePlus   web service   and   a   consumer   health   site’s   API,   both   providing   search   results   for   the   query   “diabetes.” MedlinePlus also contributes medical subject headings (MeSH) while the consumer site contributes social tags. The user sees a single search results page with the combined result set
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and Evolving Information Spaces
figures.title: Combining information with a mashup
bullets: One search draws on MedlinePlus and a consumer health service through APIs.
Medical subject headings and social tags provide complementary filters.
The interface presents a unified result set while the underlying sources remain separate.

figures.caption: Fig.2.3   Results   in   XML   format   for   the   API   query   used   in   the   health   mashup   diagrammed   in Fig.  2.3 .  https://wsearch.nlm.nih.gov/ws/query?db=healthTopics&term=%22diabetes
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and Evolving Information Spaces
figures.title: Structured data behind the interface
bullets: The XML response contains structured health-topic results for a diabetes query.
An API transfers reusable content independently of its eventual visual presentation.
This is the data layer supporting the mashup in Figure 2.2.

figures.caption: Fig.2.4   Hashtags allow for access to related topics (#ia, #library, etc.). Note the repetition of user contributed tags that mean the same thing, like “#ux” and “#userexperience”
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and Evolving Information Spaces
figures.title: Hashtags as access points
bullets: User-contributed hashtags link a post to related topics and communities.
The example uses both #ux and #userexperience for a similar concept.
Free tagging supports discovery but can fragment retrieval across synonymous labels.

figures.caption: Fig.2.5   Integrated information spaces
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Information Architecture and Evolving Information Spaces
figures.title: Integrated information spaces
bullets: Desktop, mobile, wearables, sensors, and automobiles connect to shared information spaces.
Cloud services and wireless connectivity let activities span devices and locations.
IA must support continuity across this connected ecosystem.

figures.caption: Fig.3.1   Human-centered design components: IAs should look to balance what people want or need, with the business’ ability to provide it and the technical ability to create it
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Balancing people, business, and technology
bullets: Human-centered design balances human desirability, business viability, and technical feasibility.
The overlapping circles show that useful solutions must address all three concerns.
Make competing priorities and tradeoffs explicit during design.

figures.caption: Fig.3.2   Three clouds of the HCD research
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Research, design, and evaluation
bullets: Research identifies problems and gathers evidence about people and their needs.
Design turns those findings into structures, flows, wireframes, and solutions.
Evaluation checks the design; the three activities recur throughout development.

figures.caption: Fig.3.3   Help section on an e-Commerce site with help categories and no easy “contact us” option—but links to answer common questions
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Self-service help and competing goals
bullets: The help page organizes common questions into recognizable support categories.
Self-service can reduce support costs, while users may still need direct human help.
The example illustrates a design tradeoff that depends on business priorities and user needs.

figures.caption: Fig.3.4   Detailed view of the design process with two parallel processes, front end and behind the scenes
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Two parallel design processes
bullets: Front-end work progresses from conceptual design to logical design and documentation.
Metadata, content models, and controlled vocabularies develop alongside the interface.
Usability testing feeds back into both levels; visible search depends on underlying structure.

figures.caption: Fig.3.5   Example low-ﬁdelity wireframe showing a simple product page. On the right are annota- tions that describe the functionality called out in the screen (#1, 2, 3, etc.)
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: An annotated wireframe
bullets: The low-fidelity product page emphasizes layout, filters, search, and navigation.
Numbered callouts connect interface elements to descriptions of their behavior.
Wireframes let teams discuss and test structure before committing to visual detail.

figures.caption: Fig.3.6   Example user ﬂow showing the path from a search form. The user enters a search term, and the system logic takes them to a search results page, unless the keyword is an exact content match, in which case the system takes them to the content page
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: A conditional search flow
bullets: The diagram starts with a search form and branches on an exact content match.
An exact match leads directly to content; otherwise the user sees search results.
User flows make routing decisions and expected system behavior explicit.

figures.caption: Fig.3.7   Examples of IA deliverables,  a  Blueprint and  b  Logical navigation
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Blueprint and logical navigation
bullets: Panel A maps high-level site structure; Panel B develops a more detailed navigation view.
Both diagrams communicate relationships among pages and content areas.
Use these deliverables to align the team before implementation.

figures.caption: Fig.4.1   An iterative research and evaluation process
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Research and evaluation as a cycle
bullets: The process moves through research, design, evaluation, delivery, and monitoring.
Feedback loops return later findings to earlier stages of the work.
Research continues after launch as the team learns from actual use.

figures.caption: Fig.4.2   SUS score reporting over a series of benchmarking studies on a website. 68 is the SUS average score across hundreds of sites. When do you think the redesign happened?
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Tracking perceived usability with SUS
bullets: Scores move from 66 and 63 to 68, 72, and 80 across five benchmarking rounds.
The figure uses 68 as a reference average; SUS scores are scale scores, not percentages.
The later rise suggests improvement, but the chart alone does not establish its cause.

figures.caption: Fig.4.3   Framework for a basic persona
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: A research-based persona
bullets: The template combines a biography, motivations, goals, frustrations, and technology use.
A persona represents a pattern found in research rather than an invented stereotype.
Use it to discuss audience needs and prioritize design decisions.

figures.caption: Fig.4.4   Framework for a basic user journey
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Mapping a user journey
bullets: Stages organize the persona's actions and experience over time and across touchpoints.
Quotes, emotions, and pain points connect the map to research evidence.
An opportunities row turns observed problems into potential improvements.

figures.caption: Fig.4.5   AI summarization of a recorded user interview in a user research tool
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: AI-assisted interview summaries
bullets: The tool condenses a recorded session into a short account of the main issues.
Automated summaries can help researchers review material sooner.
Check the summary against the recording or transcript before treating it as evidence.

figures.caption: Fig.4.6   AI powered interview transcription and sentiment analysis in a user research tool. Notice Yes/No to give feedback on the accuracy
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Transcription and sentiment analysis
bullets: The transcript highlights negative and positive statements from an interview.
Automated transcription and coding can speed up an initial research review.
Accuracy feedback and researcher correction remain part of the workflow.

figures.caption: Fig.5.1   A   list   of   graduate   programs.   Notice   how   the   organization   is   alphabetical,   making   the   list easily scannable
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Alphabetical organization
bullets: The graduate-program list follows an alphabetical order that users can recognize.
Predictable ordering helps people scan for a known item.
Choose an ordering method that fits the content and the user's task.

figures.caption: Fig.5.2   Sorting options often seen in e-commerce. Users may personalize the organization by selecting different items in the menu. The set of results remains the same, only the ordering changes when a new selection is made
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Sorting a result set
bullets: The menu offers price, brand, review, and recency as alternative ordering rules.
Changing the sort rearranges the same set of products.
Sorting supports different shopping goals without excluding items as a filter would.

figures.caption: Fig.5.3   A common translation feature powered by the metadata language ﬁeld
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Metadata enabling translation
bullets: A language field can help the interface offer an appropriate translation action.
The visible control depends on information describing the underlying content.
Consistent metadata connects content management to useful interface behavior.

figures.caption: Fig.5.4   Element from a metadata standard (left), and the value from a controlled vocabulary (right). Only values that are in the controlled vocabulary can be assigned to an element
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Metadata fields and controlled values
bullets: A metadata standard defines fields such as subject, date, and creator.
A controlled vocabulary supplies approved terms, such as Shirts for the subject field.
Consistent fields and values make resources easier to index and retrieve.

figures.caption: Fig.5.5   Facets on the left side of the screen (Brands and size) help the user ﬁnd their desired results
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Faceted search
bullets: Brand and size are separate facets for narrowing a product collection.
Users combine attribute choices to reduce a large result set.
Clear metadata and consistent facet labels support this targeted navigation.

figures.caption: Fig.5.6   Tags or hashtags added to a user’s post. Notice the terms preceded by the hash symbol (#) are hyperlinks. Clicking them will open a results page that have similar tags
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Tags and social classification
bullets: Hashtags turn user-chosen labels into links to other similarly tagged resources.
Collective tagging can add vocabulary beyond a centrally managed taxonomy.
Misspellings, personal labels, and synonyms can also make these collections messy.

figures.caption: Fig.5.7   Website navigation types and typical locations
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Navigation types and locations
bullets: Global navigation provides access across the site; local navigation supports a section.
Process navigation shows progress through steps; supplemental links offer additional routes.
Together these elements help people understand their location and next actions.

figures.caption: Fig.5.8   An AI agent providing assistance for potential fraud
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: An agent escalating a support task
bullets: The conversation begins with a question about a specific account charge.
The agent retains context when the user reports possible fraud.
Escalating to a human representative supports tasks requiring additional assistance.

figures.caption: Fig.6.1   The “F” shaped reading pattern, observed with eye-tracking tools in one of the author’s studies
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Human Information Behavior and Design Implications
figures.title: An F-shaped scanning pattern
bullets: The heatmap shows concentrated attention near the top and along the left side.
In this example, people scan selected areas rather than read every line.
Use clear headings and informative opening words; reading patterns vary with task and layout.

figures.caption: Fig.6.2   An Intranet site with two search boxes. Can we be sure users know which to search?
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.chapter_title: Human Information Behavior and Design Implications
figures.title: Ambiguous search scope
bullets: The intranet separates website search from a university phonebook search.
Users must decide which box covers the information they need.
Clear scope labels or a combined search with filters can reduce that uncertainty.

figures.caption: Fig.7.1   Intersection of UI design and information organization
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Interface and information organization
bullets: UI design addresses user controls and the system's responses.
Information organization addresses information elements and their connections.
The overlap shows why interaction design and IA need to work together.

figures.caption: Fig.7.2   Pagination examples demonstrating Fitts’ law
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Pagination and Fitts' law
bullets: The examples give the same page choices progressively larger visual targets.
Larger clickable areas can be easier to acquire and require less precise movement.
Design target size and spacing to reduce effort and accidental selections.

figures.caption: Fig.7.3   Typeahead functionality saves time and reduces error (misspellings)
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Typeahead for efficient input
bullets: Suggestions appear as the user begins entering a search query.
Choosing a suggestion reduces typing and can prevent misspellings.
The control helps connect the user's input to recognized destinations or terms.

figures.caption: Fig.7.4   Dialog box prevents a potential catastrophic error
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Protecting unsaved work
bullets: The dialog interrupts closing a document that contains unsaved changes.
Save, Don't Save, and Cancel make the available outcomes explicit.
A small interruption can be justified when it prevents a costly, irreversible mistake.

figures.caption: Fig.7.5   A form with instructions to help prevent errors in the password ﬁeld
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Instructions before errors occur
bullets: The example places password requirements next to the input fields.
Giving constraints before submission helps users avoid invalid entries.
The design lesson is timely guidance; the pictured rules are a historical example.

figures.caption: Fig.7.6   An error message that does not help recovery
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: An unhelpful error message
bullets: Something went wrong tells the user that an action failed without explaining why.
The message provides no specific instruction for recovery.
A useful error identifies the problem and gives a clear next step.

figures.caption: Fig.7.7   Examples of the ﬁve dimensions: 1D—The text labels; 2D—Submit button; 3D—The physical mobile device; 4D—Submitting the form, waiting for response; 5D—“Thank you!” response
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Five dimensions of interaction
bullets: Words and visual representations shape how the contact form is understood.
The physical device and time shape how the interaction unfolds.
Behavior connects the action to a visible response, here a submission confirmation.

figures.caption: Fig.7.8   Hub structure
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: A hub workflow
bullets: A central view links to several independent forms and receives the user back.
Users choose which item or task to edit instead of following a fixed sequence.
This structure suits collections such as calendars, messages, or editable records.

figures.caption: Fig.7.9   Wizard structure
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: A wizard workflow
bullets: Forms guide the user through an ordered sequence, with a possible branch.
Verification and confirmation provide checkpoints before completion.
Wizards break complex tasks into smaller steps, as in a checkout process.

figures.caption: Fig.7.10   Example page grid. As the page resizes, each container in the grid can adapt to the new screen size
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Responsive grids
bullets: The desktop grid places containers side by side; the phone view stacks them.
Breakpoints determine when the same content adopts a different arrangement.
Plan content order and grouping so the layout remains usable at each screen size.

figures.caption: Fig.7.11   An interactive element created in minutes with Bootstrap
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Reusable interface patterns
bullets: The example uses Bootstrap components for familiar tabs and a dropdown menu.
A component framework can speed implementation and support visual consistency.
Established patterns give designers a starting point that still needs to fit the task.

figures.caption: Fig.8.1   The human-centered mindset is central to human-centered design, design thinking, and systems thinking
figures.extraction: Vector artwork rendered at 360 dpi
figures.title: A shared human-centered mindset
bullets: Human-centered design, design thinking, and systems thinking share concern for people.
Zooming in helps develop specific solutions; zooming out reveals wider relationships.
Consider everyone affected by the system, including people behind the visible interface.

figures.caption: Fig.8.2   The design thinking process from stanford’s d.school, with an Implement stage added
figures.extraction: Vector artwork rendered at 360 dpi
figures.title: From empathy to implementation
bullets: The sequence covers Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test, and Implement.
The authors add implementation to show that the outcome must work in practice.
Although drawn as a line, the process repeatedly revisits earlier stages.

figures.caption: Fig.8.3   The system mapping team. Core team members do most of the work, with extended stepping in from time to time. Participants are called in more infrequently, at key moments
figures.extraction: Vector artwork rendered at 360 dpi
figures.title: A system-mapping team
bullets: The core team performs the day-to-day mapping work.
Extended team members contribute subject expertise on a regular basis.
Other participants join at key moments to supply additional perspectives.

figures.caption: Fig.8.4   The   knowledge   talent   acquisition   system   map.   The   map   gives   a   clear   view   of   the   system for   leaders   and   individual   contributors.   Taking   a   human-centered   approach,   the   blue   lines   on   this map   highlight   AI,   automation,   and   usability   components   that   directly   inﬂuence   the   work   practices of people in the system
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: A talent-acquisition system map
bullets: The central concern is the efficiency of hiring the best-fit candidate.
Connected elements show dependencies across candidate, recruiter, and organizational activities.
Blue links highlight AI, automation, and usability contributions; the map helps locate leverage points.

figures.caption: Fig.9.1   User experience design disciplines peaks and valleys in the HCD process
figures.extraction: Embedded raster image extracted at original resolution
figures.title: Changing effort across the HCD process
bullets: The curves illustrate changing involvement by IA, research, visual, and interaction design.
IA effort is strongest early; researchers return for successive rounds of testing.
These overlapping patterns support coordination rather than rigid handoffs between roles.

figures.caption: Fig.9.2   Teams and roles in the HCD process
figures.extraction: Vector artwork rendered at 360 dpi
figures.title: Connecting users, technology, and business
bullets: The UX team represents user concerns alongside technology and business stakeholders.
Developers, IT teams, product owners, analysts, and executives bring different priorities.
Explain design decisions in terms that connect user outcomes to technical and business goals.
